escalate

/ES-kuh-layt/ - the stress falls on ES · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Escalate means to rise, or make something rise, level by level — a conflict, demand, or cost climbing by stages, each more serious than the last.

The referee stepped between the two captains before the shoving could escalate into something the league would have to review.

Example

What began as a quarrel over a hedge escalated by degrees: clipped remarks in the driveway, then surveyor's stakes, then a letter from a lawyer, until two households that had traded casseroles for a decade stopped waving.

Escalate is the ladder verb: trouble that escalates does not merely grow, it moves up rungs — remark to stake to lawyer — and every rung climbed is harder to climb back down. That stepwise rise, level by named level, is what separates escalating from simply getting worse.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

intensify: to grow stronger or more extreme in degree — heat, pressure, or feeling turned up. Escalate climbs by stages instead: each level passed makes the next one likelier.

mount: to build up gradually — mounting bills, mounting evidence, a quiet accumulation. Escalate is mount with a threat in it: the rise runs level by level toward a breaking point.

aggravate: to make an existing problem worse — aggravate an injury, an insult that aggravates a feud. Escalate is about height, not just harm: the trouble moves up to a more serious plane.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

defuse: to take the danger out of a situation before it goes off

subside: to sink back down toward calm

Where it sits · how steeply the trouble climbs

mount → escalate → spiral

mount vs. escalate: Mount is weaker than escalate — mounting tension gathers quietly in the background, while escalating tension is already climbing from level to level in plain view.

spiral vs. escalate: Spiral is stronger than escalate — an escalating conflict still climbs one rung at a time, but a spiraling one has slipped its handlers and feeds on itself faster than anyone can respond.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — escal: ladder (Latin scala; Romance spelling grew an e- in front)

Suffix — -ate: verb: to make or become

Put it together: Escal- (Latin scala, 'ladder,' wearing the e- that Spanish and French grew in front of it) + -ate (to make or become) = to ladder. English got the verb from a machine: the escalator, the moving stair named around 1900, was clipped back to escalate — first meaning to ride the stairs, then, in the Cold War years, to climb rung by rung into a bigger conflict.

Use the root in a new word: echelon: The scandal never spread beyond a single echelon of the ministry — those above it never learned, and those below never guessed.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral — news, business, and diplomatic writing

Escalate frames a rise as a climb up identifiable levels, which is why it dominates reporting on conflicts, disputes, and prices: each step can be named, and each is harder to reverse. When something merely grows stronger with no rungs to point to, intensify is the more accurate verb; and when you raise a problem to a higher authority on purpose — 'escalate the ticket' — the word is doing its ladder work in an office instead of a war room.
